CD Projekt Red: If you want a cost-driven development, you cannot make The Witcher 4
Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski on making multiple projects, the console market, and returning to The Witcher 3
Christopher Dring
Sep 01, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
CD Projekt Red joint CEO Michał Nowakowski on…
Making multiple projects
Returning to The Witcher 3
State of consoles
Plus, discs, Unreal Engine, Switch 2, TV shows, and more
Death is the great motivator. And it’s certainly motivating CD Projekt Red.
For 20 years, The Witcher developer has worked on one major project at a time. But today, it’s making three. There’s The Witcher 4, due in 2028, a sequel to Cyberpunk and a new IP called Project Hadar.
“Everybody has a biology built into them. We were like, ‘if we keep doing things the way we do, and we have a lot of ideas, we’re only going to make X, Y, Z before we retire, or naturally retire from this place’,” says CD Projekt Red joint CEO Michał Nowakowski on today’s The Game Business Show .
“So how can we do more, but not compromise on quality? This was the predominant thought behind that. And then we started thinking, ‘Okay, what’s the business around that?’ This is my biggest wish. I’d like us to look back and say, ‘Okay, we did it, we told two, three stories instead of just one within that moment, and all of them were top-notch’.”
The cynic might suggest that there’s another, more commercial reason why CD Projekt Red would want to develop multiple major games at once. But Nowakowski believes financial growth isn’t entirely down to making more games. The Witcher 3 may now be on 65 million sales, with Cyberpunk 2077 on 40 million, but there’s room to sell more, he says.
“If you look at what GTA V sold, these are very different numbers to what we have achieved. There is still room for growth.”
There is another option to getting more games out, and that’s to simply make them faster. Not only would that allow CD Projekt Red to release more, it’d also help bring down costs. But it’s not how the studio thinks.
“We are cost-conscious,” Nowakowski explains. “It’s not unimportant. We’re a business in the end. But the first thing is whether the qualityis there, period. This is the dominant thing we look at.
“I definitely wouldn’t put cost in the number one position, as weird as that may sound. We try to make sure we’re within the boundaries, or if it’s exceeding, then we sit down and think what it means for everything. But I definitely wouldn’t say this is a cost-driven development. If you want to have a cost-driven development, and that’s a proper business thinking for a lot of games, you cannot make a game like The Witcher 4. I doubt if the development of GTA VI was a cost-driven development. In fact, I’m 100% sure it wasn’t.”
Nevertheless, to achieve the goal of multiple projects does require a technical rethink. The developer has walked away from its REDengine, which powered The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077, in favour of Unreal Engine. Nowakowski tells us that REDengine needed starting from scratch with each new release. By moving to Unreal, it should make switching between projects simpler.
Initially, there will be some pain. Pipelines and tools will need reworking and changing. But the bigger threat from this technical pivot is whether using an off-the-shelf engine might negatively impact the uniqueness of the games.
“That was a big question we were asking ourselves, because pushing the envelope with how the games look, the cinematic feel of it all, is very, very important,” Nowakowski answers. “And that was a big question mark when we were in the R&D phase over whether Unreal Engine 5 is going to be a good fit or not. We really asked ourselves all of these questions, and in some cases the answer was, ‘not yet.’
“But together with Epic, we can bring it to that point. I know when we made that switch, people were saying, ‘Oh, it’s going to be another Unreal-looking game.’ But we’re not going to be. We really are going to be able to differentiate ourselves. People are going to feel this is a CDPR game still, and the technology under the hood is actually going to be irrelevant from a pure fan perspective.”
In today’s edition of The Game Business Show, Nowakowski expands on CD Projekt’s multi-game vision, discusses the state of consoles, Cyberpunk 2077’s Switch 2 launch, TV and movie adaptations, The Witcher 3 Remastered, and more. You can watch the full conversation above, or check out extra highlights below.
Sponsored Message
Game Development, built to scale
Keywords Studios is the games industry’s end-to-end partner, with over 13,000 people across 26 countries helping studios build, launch and grow games at global scale. Supercharged by technology and shaped by long-term partnership, Keywords Studios connects specialist expertise around the player experience.
For game development, that means flexible production support that scales with ambition. From co-development and engineering to live operations and technical delivery, Keywords Studios helps teams move faster, solve complexity and keep production connected, without losing sight of the game players are waiting for.
CD Projekt Red never considered charging for The Witcher 3 Remastered
It may be 11 years-old, but The Witcher 3 was the most viewed game at this year’s Gamescom.
CD Projekt Red announced a fully remastered version of the game, which will surprise launch in less than a month. What’s more, The Witcher 3 Remastered is a free upgrade for existing Witcher 3 owners. It’s a generous offer. But surely fans would have been willing to pay for it?
“It was never a question we asked ourselves,” Nowakowski tells us. “We were going deeper into the development of Songs of the Past with [developer] Fool’s Theory, and we started chatting: ‘Why don’t we make the game more modern? Everything felt like it was developed 10 years ago’. Because it was developed more than 10 years ago.
“We started chatting about what we could do to improve it. It started with small things and then it turned into this larger project, and we suddenly realized we had a remaster on our hands.
“But coming back to your original commercial question, we never thought about it this way. The commercial bit is the expansion, but with the game, we really felt this is the CDPR way to gift it to the players who already own it. It was just never a question we asked ourselves.”
As Nowakowski says, the remaster is the precursor for Songs of the Past, which is the first The Witcher 3 expansion in over a decade.
“We felt that The Witcher 3 was a closed book and we’d never come back to it,” Nowakowski admits. “But a couple of happy accidents happened. We started a collaboration with Fool’s Theory. They were supposed to work on The Witcher 1 [remake], but we realized that needed a bit more time because of certain technology dependencies with The Witcher 4.
“We actually had the idea for a third expansion a long time ago, but it was put in a drawer forever. We never thought we’d be taking it out. But one conversation led to another, which led to, ‘Why don’t we make an expansion?’ Does it even make sense after such a long time? Has anybody done that for a single-player game? That led us to, ‘It sounds crazy, but let’s give Geralt one more ride’.”
It may sound unusual, but it’s somewhat fitting with CD Projekt Red, which likes to create ‘moments’ that bring players back to its games. Whether that’s DLC, or a spin-off, or a TV adaptation.
“I was told by someone, ‘You guys are kind of live-operating a single-player game.’ And I laughed a little, but actually, that person has a point. We create these moments that bring in new people.”
Investors didn’t force the launch Cyberpunk 2077
The Witcher 3 sold five million copies over the last year, and Cyberpunk 2077 sold even more. Not bad for games that are 11 and six years-old respectively.
I asked Nowakowski if this takes the financial pressure off having to hit certain deadlines for games like The Witcher 4. I pointed to the disastrous launch of Cyberpunk 2077, which was released before it was ready in December 2020.
“That situation was different,” he explains. “First of all, we were in a very peculiar moment in the middle of COVID. And the way tension built within the team was a bit different than if that hadn’t been the case. I don’t want to put it all on COVID, but it was a factor. The team was getting exhausted in a different way. There were people outside telling us we should launch, fans asking for it, but the team itself also wanted to push it out the door because it was really tiring at that moment in time.
“The decision to launch was for sure wrong, period. There’s no denying it. But there were no magical investors telling us, ‘you have to get this out’. It was much more complicated and psychological.”
“Consoles will weather the storm”
CD Projekt Red performs strongly on Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo. And over the years, it’s had partnerships with all three platform holders.
So, I had to ask how Nowakowski felt about the current situation facing the console sector, where rising costs is forcing prices up, and potentially impacting sales.
“I’m not worried,” he says. “Consoles are still necessary to broaden the audience on the casual or semi-casual level. It’s important to have easy to plug in and enjoy gaming.
“I’m big believer that they’re going to weather the storm. Pricing is the objective challenge. And the rumors... we hear them about the next-gen being delayed. I don’t know if they’re true.”
Is it a problem if Xbox Project Helix and PS6 take longer to arrive?
“How we reach gamers is a little irrelevant. Content is the king. And if the content is right, people will find a way to play it,” Nowakowski says.
“When we launch, if PS5, Xbox Series X/S is what people are playing, we’re going to be there. We’re going to find a business model that’s going to work for us, that’s going to be fine for players, and that’s it.
“If you ask the dev team, they will always answer: ‘Give us as much power as you can because we want to show off the best stuff.’ That’s the way they’re wired. But they’re realistic. If the next-gen gets delayed, it could be the case that some ideas are put on a shelf for the future. We’d have to adjust. We’re not worried on the commercial side. Consoles are here to stay.”
“We kill a lot of ideas”
Going back to the start, CD Projekt Red wants to get to a point where it can launch “two, three games within a relatively short period of time.”
“It’s three isolated teams with clear leadership, with clear vision,” says Nowakowski. “And there’s a certain capacity beyond which we cannot go if we want to be sure that we deliver at a certain level.”
That’s the crucial bit. CD Projekt Red has always had side projects, but working on three major games at the same time risks losing some focus.
“ There is always a risk,” Nowakowski concludes. “And we actually kill a lot of ideas, because we believe we cannot execute them with a proper focus. Every development, every collaboration, every partnership we make, we go into that with the thought about whether we can actually deliver on it.
“Even external, especially external actually, we invest our people in being part of the process, making sure that the other side understands what The Witcher or Cyberpunk is. We have a franchise team specifically working just on that, to make sure that it sticks to the story or lore, that the visuals fall within what we think is fitting for The Witcher or Cyberpunk, and so on. A lot of scrutiny goes into that.
“We would love to do more. It’s just there’s a limit to what we can do. Because if we go larger, everything’s going to fall apart.”
Check out our full interview with Nowakowski above.
That’s it for today. Join us on Thursday with our next big edition, which dives into the latest Newzoo report, and the potential wider industry impact of GTA 6. Until then, thank you for reading.

title: Game Oracle v6.4.0: a clearer view of where the market is moving
author: Ross Burton, PhD
text:
Game Oracle v6.4.0: a clearer view of where the market is moving
Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Devlogs
Published: 9/1/2026
Updated: 8/24/2026
Game Oracle v6.4.0 is one of our biggest releases yet. It introduces a ground-up rebuild of Game Gap, two new dashboard features for finding fast-moving trends and promising opportunities, a more robust projection model for Concept Compass, and a clearer way to read momentum across Steam Map.
The theme connecting all of these changes is simple: better signals, with less noise .
Steam is a huge, fast-moving market. A useful research tool cannot just show you more data; it needs to help you understand which games genuinely compete with one another, where player interest is building, and how much confidence you should place in the result. v6.4.0 is a major step in that direction.
Game Gap has been rebuilt from the ground up
Game Gap exists to answer a difficult question: where is there meaningful player demand without an equally strong supply of games serving it?
The quality of that answer depends on the quality of the market segments underneath it. If a segment is too broad, unrelated games blur together and its statistics become difficult to act on. If it is too narrow, it stops representing a real market. Steam games also rarely fit inside one neat genre box: a game might be a deckbuilder, a roguelite, a management game and a cosy game at the same time.
For v6.4.0, we have replaced Game Gap's original clustering system with an entirely new algorithm.
The new system first looks at the Steam catalogue through three lenses: 2D , 3D , and an inclusive Both view. It then uses genres and themes to build looser areas of the market before finding overlapping groups of games within them. Because the groups can overlap, a game can appear in more than one legitimate market context instead of being forced into a single category.
One of the most important changes is a new hubness penalty . In a large catalogue, some broadly relevant games can appear similar to an enormous number of other titles. Left unchecked, those games become bridges between otherwise distinct markets, pulling specific niches into vague, generic clusters. The new algorithm recognises and reduces the influence of those hubs while preserving genuinely useful connections.
We have also redesigned the wider clustering process to account for local context and the stability of each group. In plain English, it asks more than “do these two games sound similar?” It also considers whether they occupy the same meaningful neighbourhood of the market and whether the segment remains coherent when viewed in different ways.
The precise weighting and thresholds stay under the hood. What matters in the product is the result: **more refined, more coherent and more actionable market segments**, with better protection against generic titles distorting a niche.
The Game Gap interface has received a substantial upgrade alongside the new model:
- A new Both / 2D / 3D market lens, with Both providing the broadest view of the catalogue.
- New keyword search, filters and sorting options, including sorting by Top Picks, demand, uniqueness or median sales.
- Improved navigation within segment detail pages, making long reports easier to move through.
- Clearer segment cards and improved ways to explore warnings, market composition and performance.
- Reintroduced Game Gap Opportunities links on game detail pages. When a game belongs to a market segment, you can now jump directly from that game into the relevant opportunity.
The last point is particularly useful in practice. Research does not always begin with a market category; often it begins with a game. The new backlinks let you start with a title you know and move directly into the wider markets around it.
Introducing Trend Watch
It is useful to know what has performed well historically. It is just as important to see what is beginning to move now.
Trend Watch is a new dashboard view of the strongest themes among Steam's popular upcoming games and recent top sellers. It combines Steam's Popular Upcoming list with top-selling releases from the last 30 days, then groups closely related games into focused trend clusters.
Each cluster shows the games moving together and the genres, themes or ideas they share. Coming-soon games are shown with estimated wishlist momentum, while released games are shown with estimated sales momentum. This makes it easier to distinguish a broader pattern from a single breakout title.
Trend Watch is designed to be selective. Two games mentioning the same broad genre does not automatically make them a trend. The system uses the wider Steam catalogue as context to look for groups with stronger evidence that they occupy the same part of the market. That lets it surface specific patterns without filling the dashboard with loose combinations of generically similar games.
The ordering is also personalised. As you save Concept Compass projects, bookmark games or Game Gap segments, and use Data Explorer, Trend Watch increasingly prioritises trends related to the markets you are researching. Everyone can still see what is gaining momentum across Steam; the most relevant signals simply rise towards the top.
You can also opt into a monthly Trend Watch email , bringing a personalised summary of the market to your inbox. It is entirely optional and can be managed from the new email preference centre.
Introducing Top Opportunities
Trend Watch answers “what is building momentum?” Top Opportunities answers “where should I investigate next?”
Top Opportunities is a new dashboard shortlist of up to three Game Gap market segments combining strong demand with relatively low competition. It uses the familiar Game Gap cards, including demand and uniqueness scores, median sales or wishlists where available, market composition and important warning flags.
Like Trend Watch, the shortlist becomes more relevant as you use Game Oracle. Your concepts, bookmarks and Data Explorer history help bring suitable opportunities forward. If there is not enough personal research history yet, the dashboard falls back to some of the strongest opportunities across Steam.
This is not intended to replace a full Game Gap investigation. It is a starting point: a quick, useful shortlist that can lead directly into the complete segment analysis when something catches your attention.
A more robust projection model for Concept Compass
Concept Compass projections have been rebuilt around a new Bayesian model .
Forecasting a game's potential from comparable titles is difficult because Steam outcomes are extremely uneven. A handful of breakout hits can distort simple averages, while a long tail of abandoned, experimental or minimally marketed releases can make a serious commercial project look less viable than the evidence suggests. The apparent precision of a forecast can also be misleading when the available competitors are only weakly related to the concept.
The new model is more critical about which competitors are allowed to influence a projection and how much influence each one receives. It measures competitors on a consistent similarity scale, separates unreleased games from realised post-release outcomes, and excludes evidence that is too new, incomplete or unrepresentative for the question being asked.
It then balances the evidence from genuinely comparable games with a wider baseline of commercial Steam releases. When the concept has several strong comparables, those games contribute more to the projection. When evidence is limited, the model relies more on the wider baseline and communicates that uncertainty through the projected range rather than pretending to know more than it does.
The result is not a promise of performance. Execution, marketing, timing and product quality still matter enormously. It is a more defensible estimate of the range a genuine commercial launch could occupy, built from competitors that better represent the market you are actually entering.
Concept Compass has also gained several workflow and report improvements:
Progressive loading: the competitor landscape becomes available first, while resource suggestions, marketing content, the competition summary and player sentiment continue loading independently in the background.
Automatic drafts: once you begin naming a project, your progress is saved as a draft so you can leave the wizard and return without losing your work.
Player sentiment: a new summary of what players like and dislike across relevant competitor reviews.
Competition summary: a concise overview of the competitive landscape around your idea.
Suggested publishers: a new list of real publishers behind comparable games, giving you more relevant outreach targets to research.
Together, these changes make Concept Compass faster to start using, harder to lose work in, and more useful beyond the headline projections.

We have completely redesigned the presentation of trend data in Steam Map.
Previously, it was too easy to read a colour or percentage without enough context and reach the wrong conclusion. The new Trends view makes a clearer distinction between three questions:
Supply: where new Steam listings are increasing.
Demand: where wishlist and sales momentum are strongest.
Opportunities: where demand is growing favourably relative to new competition.
Trend colours now describe the selected market cluster consistently, while the underlying map still preserves the more detailed shape of that market. Growth figures use the median so one extreme success cannot speak for an entire cluster, and each result is compared with the Steam-wide median over the same period.
That comparison is really important. A market can be growing in absolute terms and still rank below the rest of Steam. Likewise, an increase in new games is positive when you are examining supply, but it can be a warning when you are looking for an opportunity with limited incoming competition.

A more useful dashboard
The dashboard has been reorganised around a new layout and table of contents, so it is easier to move between Trend Watch, Top Opportunities, bookmarks, product shortcuts and updates.
There is also a new Discord updates section showing recent posts from our #platform-updates channel. You can now keep up with product changes from inside Game Oracle or jump into the Discord conversation for more detail.
As part of simplifying the product, we have retired the onboarding checklist and Bundle Builder. Engagement with both was low, and removing them creates a clearer path into the tools people use most.
Clearer email choices
v6.4.0 introduces clearer consent around marketing emails and a centralised Email Preference Centre  in Account Settings.
This gives you one place to manage the updates you want to receive, including the optional monthly Trend Watch report. The aim is straightforward: useful communication, chosen by you, with preferences that are easy to understand and change.
Fixes and polish
This release also includes a broad set of fixes across the platform:
Improved the formatting and readability of summaries on game detail pages.
Removed free-to-play games from median Steam sales and revenue figures on developer and publisher pages, where they were creating misleading comparisons.
Fixed errors and state issues in several welcome tours.
Fixed free-tier Steam Map title search breaking page scrolling.
Fixed Data Explorer searches containing multiple tags.
Fixed an intermittent issue where the first navbar search result click did not open the selected game, developer or publisher page.
Corrected wishlist-change and sales-change statistics affected by a numerical error in the data pipeline.
Repaired several broken mobile layouts.
Preserved referral links through login so users arrive at the page they originally requested instead of being redirected to the dashboard.
One connected research workflow
The biggest change in v6.4.0 is not any single card, score or interface. It is how the tools now work together.
You can spot a pattern forming in Trend Watch, investigate the surrounding market in Game Gap, test a specific idea in Concept Compass, and use Top Opportunities to return to the most promising areas. Steam Map provides the wider momentum context, while personalisation uses the research you save across Game Oracle to make the next signal more relevant.
We are excited to put v6.4.0 out there. As always, estimates are evidence for a decision rather than a substitute for one, but we hope this release gives you stronger evidence, clearer context and a much better place to begin.

Game Oracle v6.4.0: a clearer view of where the market is moving

Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Devlogs
Published: 9/1/2026
Updated: 8/24/2026

Game Oracle v6.4.0 is one of our biggest releases yet. It introduces a ground-up rebuild of Game Gap, two new dashboard features for finding fast-moving trends and promising opportunities, a more robust projection model for Concept Compass, and a clearer way to read momentum across Steam Map.

The theme connecting all of these changes is simple: better signals, with less noise.

Steam is a huge, fast-moving market. A useful research tool cannot just show you more data; it needs to help you understand which games genuinely compete with one another, where player interest is building, and how much confidence you should place in the result. v6.4.0 is a major step in that direction.

Game Gap has been rebuilt from the ground up

Game Gap exists to answer a difficult question: where is there meaningful player demand without an equally strong supply of games serving it?

The quality of that answer depends on the quality of the market segments underneath it. If a segment is too broad, unrelated games blur together and its statistics become difficult to act on. If it is too narrow, it stops representing a real market. Steam games also rarely fit inside one neat genre box: a game might be a deckbuilder, a roguelite, a management game and a cosy game at the same time.

For v6.4.0, we have replaced Game Gap's original clustering system with an entirely new algorithm.

The new system first looks at the Steam catalogue through three lenses: 2D, 3D, and an inclusive Both view. It then uses genres and themes to build looser areas of the market before finding overlapping groups of games within them. Because the groups can overlap, a game can appear in more than one legitimate market context instead of being forced into a single category.

One of the most important changes is a new hubness penalty. In a large catalogue, some broadly relevant games can appear similar to an enormous number of other titles. Left unchecked, those games become bridges between otherwise distinct markets, pulling specific niches into vague, generic clusters. The new algorithm recognises and reduces the influence of those hubs while preserving genuinely useful connections.

We have also redesigned the wider clustering process to account for local context and the stability of each group. In plain English, it asks more than “do these two games sound similar?” It also considers whether they occupy the same meaningful neighbourhood of the market and whether the segment remains coherent when viewed in different ways.

The precise weighting and thresholds stay under the hood. What matters in the product is the result: **more refined, more coherent and more actionable market segments**, with better protection against generic titles distorting a niche.

The Game Gap interface has received a substantial upgrade alongside the new model:

- A new Both / 2D / 3D market lens, with Both providing the broadest view of the catalogue.
- New keyword search, filters and sorting options, including sorting by Top Picks, demand, uniqueness or median sales.
- Improved navigation within segment detail pages, making long reports easier to move through.
- Clearer segment cards and improved ways to explore warnings, market composition and performance.
- Reintroduced Game Gap Opportunities links on game detail pages. When a game belongs to a market segment, you can now jump directly from that game into the relevant opportunity.

The last point is particularly useful in practice. Research does not always begin with a market category; often it begins with a game. The new backlinks let you start with a title you know and move directly into the wider markets around it.

Introducing Trend Watch

It is useful to know what has performed well historically. It is just as important to see what is beginning to move now.

Trend Watch is a new dashboard view of the strongest themes among Steam's popular upcoming games and recent top sellers. It combines Steam's Popular Upcoming list with top-selling releases from the last 30 days, then groups closely related games into focused trend clusters.

Trend Watch is designed to be selective. Two games mentioning the same broad genre does not automatically make them a trend. The system uses the wider Steam catalogue as context to look for groups with stronger evidence that they occupy the same part of the market. That lets it surface specific patterns without filling the dashboard with loose combinations of generically similar games.

The ordering is also personalised. As you save Concept Compass projects, bookmark games or Game Gap segments, and use Data Explorer, Trend Watch increasingly prioritises trends related to the markets you are researching. title: 游戏深度分析：广告变现洞察报告
author: Sensor Tower
text:
移动广告变现已经成为游戏行业大多数产品的重要商业模式。支持广告变现的游戏仍贡献了绝大多数游戏下载量。这意味着，广告策略已不再只是辅助变现手段，而是逐渐成为覆盖更广泛市场、帮助游戏获取和提升用户参与度的重要基础。
要理解移动游戏广告变现市场，需要先看清其明显的结构性差异。游戏广告收入高度集中于少数品类、广告网络和产品模式，市场结构呈现出明显差异。解谜类游戏仍是移动游戏广告变现收入的主要来源，而广告网络的选择，也会影响不同游戏品类与广告主需求及目标用户之间的匹配效率。对于混合休闲游戏而言，是以广告变现还是 IAP 为核心，同样是一项关键的商业决策，并将直接影响产品的收入上限。
总体来看，这是一个规模超过 120亿美元 、已经较为成熟的市场。要在其中取得成功，需要将游戏设计、区域市场选择和整体运营策略更好地结合起来。 下载 Sensor Tower《游戏深度分析：广告变现洞察报告》 ，获取完整分析。
广告变现游戏仍主导游戏下载市场
分析移动游戏的用户进入路径时，需要重点关注下载量而非收入，因为在全球主要市场中，支持广告变现的游戏仍贡献了绝大多数下载量。虽然这一比例较历史高点略有下降，但其长期稳定性更值得关注：即使应用内购（IAP）增长放缓，且新一代解谜和混合休闲玩法不断改变竞争格局，广告变现游戏的主导地位依然稳固。
这一格局的形成，并不意味着广告变现游戏数量大幅增加，而更多是因为非广告变现游戏逐渐减少。广告变现也并非要取代 IAP，而是为发行商提供了一种触达并留住更广泛、更多元用户群体的常规手段。因此，对于如今的移动游戏而言，游戏分发与广告策略正日益融为一体。许多高下载量产品从立项之初就将广告融入玩法和成长体系，而不是在产品上线后再作为辅助功能加入。
解谜类游戏在主流广告网络中普遍占据广告收入主导地位
在多数大型广告网络中，解谜类游戏贡献了超过一半的广告变现收入，街机、模拟和桌游类游戏则构成其余收入的大部分。无论广告网络更擅长高频插屏广告和激励视频广告，还是覆盖更广泛的休闲游戏用户群体，这一收入集中趋势都较为明显。
少数例外情况并非随机波动，而是源于各广告网络的历史发行商合作关系及其全球覆盖范围的差异。部分网络的品类分布更为均衡，或对街机类广告库存有更明显的侧重。对于广告主而言，这意味着他们所购买的广告展示中，有相当大一部分会触达解谜类游戏用户。对于非解谜类游戏发行商而言，选择广告网络已不仅仅是程序化变现的收益优化问题，更核心的问题是，其游戏品类是否符合该广告网络广告主的需求结构。
混合休闲已分化为两种模式，收入表现存在明显差异
混合休闲市场已形成两种不同的变现模式。 广告优先型产品的收入绝大部分来自广告，这为其提供了相对稳定且易于规模化的变现基础。相比之下，IAP优先型产品则在广告之外构建了完整的付费经济体系，应用内购贡献了收入的大部分。虽然两类产品都属于混合休闲，但最终的收入表现存在明显差异。
以 IAP 为主的产品，其收入通常明显高于以广告为主的产品。广告变现能够提供相对稳定的收入基础，而 IAP 则往往能够进一步抬高产品的收入上限。因此，发行商在设计混合休闲产品时，需要尽早确定主要增长模式：是围绕高价值用户付费打造产品循环，还是以广告展示量和规模化用户获取为核心。
广告变现已经不再是移动游戏中的辅助选项。其影响着玩家发现游戏的方式、广告需求向何处集中，以及混合休闲游戏能够实现多大的增长规模。那些在此取得成功的团队，其产品设计正是顺应了这一现实，而非仅仅停留在广告聚合策略的调整上。
如需按市场、广告网络、品类及游戏维度查看详细数据拆解， 欢迎阅读完整《游戏深度分析：广告变现洞察报告》。

解谜类游戏在主流广告网络中普遍占据广告收入主导地位

在多数大型广告网络中，解谜类游戏贡献了超过一半的广告变现收入，街机、模拟和桌游类游戏则构成其余收入的大部分。无论广告网络更擅长高频插屏广告和激励视频广告，还是覆盖更广泛的休闲游戏用户群体，这一收入集中趋势都较为明显。

少数例外情况并非随机波动，而是源于各广告网络的历史发行商合作关系及其全球覆盖范围的差异。部分网络的品类分布更为均衡，或对街机类广告库存有更明显的侧重。对于广告主而言，这意味着他们所购买的广告展示中，有相当大一部分会触达解谜类游戏用户。对于非解谜类游戏发行商而言，选择广告网络已不仅仅是程序化变现的收益优化问题，更核心的问题是，其游戏品类是否符合该广告网络广告主的需求结构。

混合休闲已分化为两种模式，收入表现存在明显差异

混合休闲市场已形成两种不同的变现模式。 广告优先型产品的收入绝大部分来自广告，这为其提供了相对稳定且易于规模化的变现基础。相比之下，IAP优先型产品则在广告之外构建了完整的付费经济体系，应用内购贡献了收入的大部分。虽然两类产品都属于混合休闲，但最终的收入表现存在明显差异。

以 IAP 为主的产品，其收入通常明显高于以广告为主的产品。广告变现能够提供相对稳定的收入基础，而 IAP 则往往能够进一步抬高产品的收入上限。因此，发行商在设计混合休闲产品时，需要尽早确定主要增长模式：是围绕高价值用户付费打造产品循环，还是以广告展示量和规模化用户获取为核心。

广告变现已经不再是移动游戏中的辅助选项。其影响着玩家发现游戏的方式、广告需求向何处集中，以及混合休闲游戏能够实现多大的增长规模。那些在此取得成功的团队，其产品设计正是顺应了这一现实，而非仅仅停留在广告聚合策略的调整上。
